  <p class="overview-kicker">Arct et al. 2026</p>
  <h1>Warmer springs are associated with larger clutches but lower egg-to-fledging success in a migratory passerine</h1>
  </div>
</div>

<section class="overview-intro">
  <h2><span class="section-number">0.1</span> Study aims</h2>
  <p>We asked how spring temperature was associated with reproductive performance in the collared flycatcher, and whether these responses were expressed through changes in average performance, reproductive consistency, or both.</p>
  <p>Specifically, we examined:</p>
  <ul>
    <li>whether mean spring temperature and residual interannual variability changed through time;</li>
    <li>clutch size and its conditional consistency among breeding attempts were associated with spring temperature, relative laying date, female age, and long-term time;</li>
    <li>fledging success and its conditional consistency among breeding attempts were associated with spring temperature, relative laying date, female age, and long-term time.</li>
  </ul>
<p><strong>Current manuscript results.</strong> Mean temperature increased by 0.0439°C per year (95% CI [0.0248, 0.0630]). Warmer springs were associated with larger clutches and lower egg-to-fledging success. The reference model includes year random effects in both components and provides no clear evidence of a temperature association with fledging consistency. No clear temperature association with clutch-size inconsistency was detected. Scale effects describe heterogeneity among breeding attempts, not within-female repeatability.</p>
</section>
